name: Vāgaṛī / वागड़ी
confidence_why: Joshi 1964, the only phonology that gives placement rules, describes a weak, predictable word stress drawn to the syllable before a consonant cluster and otherwise to the penult (with a final-syllable exception for words ending in e or o), and Vyas 1967's remark for the Dungarpur variety that stress is not distinctive is compatible with that rather than against it, while Mukherjee 2011, Phillips 2012 and Grierson 1907 say nothing about stress.

catalog_quote: हम जब वागड़ी की बात करते हैं तब मुख्यतया शब्दगत स्वराघात के बलात्मक स्वरभार की क्या स्थिति है वह देख लेनी चाहिए। ... वह मृदु भी है और एक ही शब्द में, वर्णों की वृद्धि के कारण, स्थानच्युत भी बनता है। ... १. एक श्रुतिवाले शब्दों में स्वर सर्वदा बलात्मक स्वरभार युक्त है ... २. एक से ज्यादा श्रुतिवाले शब्दों में संयुक्त व्यंजन के पूर्व का स्वर सदा बलात्मक स्वरभार युक्त है -- अद्दर, लुस्सौ, गुँस्सौ, एवं अनुनासिक व्यंजनों वाले रंग, भंग, संपल, कुंदोई, जैसे शब्द. ... ३. अ:- दो श्रुतिवाले शब्दों में अंतिम श्रुति शांत (silent) अ वाली है अथवा तो खुले इ-उ वाली है, तब उपान्त्यस्वर पर ही भार आता है -- वात, खार, ... आ:- द्वि श्रुतिवाले शब्दों में यदि अंत में ए-ओ आते हैं और पूर्व की श्रुति में अ-इ-उ होते हैं तब अंतिम ए-ओ पर ही भार आता है -- करे, मरे, ... करौ, मरौ, ... ४.:- तीन श्रुति वाले शब्दों में प्राथमिक स्वरभार सामान्यतया आदि श्रुति में और द्वैतीयिक स्वरभार अंतिम श्रुति में रहता है -- ..., दिकरौ, सतरि / जबकि आदि श्रुति में अ-इ-उ होते हैं और द्वितीय श्रुति में आ-ए-ओ आते हैं तब द्वितीय श्रुति में ही भार निहित होता है। दलासौ, बलाडु, कुँवारु, ... आरोहावरोहात्मक स्वरभार (Pitch accent) सर्वथा वाक्यगत है और अर्थानुसारी है

new_statements.translation: 2. In words of more than one syllable the vowel before a conjunct consonant always carries the stress [...] 3(a). In disyllabic words whose final syllable has silent a or open i/u, the stress falls on the penultimate vowel [...] 3(b). In disyllabic words, if e/o comes at the end and the preceding syllable has a/i/u, the stress falls on the final e/o -- kare, mare [...] 4. In trisyllabic words the primary stress is generally on the initial syllable and the secondary stress on the final syllable -- kutru, dikro, satri. But when the initial syllable has a/i/u and the second syllable has aa/e/o, the stress rests on the second syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Weak, non-contrastive dynamic stress whose position depends on vowel quality/quantity and syllable closure: monosyllables are stressed; a vowel followed by a consonant cluster (incl. nasal+C) is stressed; otherwise in disyllables stress is on the first (penultimate) syllable unless the first has a short vowel (a, i, u) and the second a full vowel (e, o), in which case the final is stressed; in trisyllables primary stress is initial with secondary on the final, unless the first syllable has a/i/u and the second has aa/e/o, in which case the second syllable is stressed. I.e. stress the leftmost heavy (long-vowel or closed) syllable within the first two, default initial.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In trisyllables secondary stress on the final syllable when primary is initial (p.48 rule 4); p.47: 'secondary stress is also expressed in longer words as appropriate'; with a/i/u first syllable + Cy cluster the y-syllable takes the stress, with aa/e/o first syllable the y-syllable takes only secondary stress (kaadyu, maansu).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is 'mild' and shifts when syllables are added (aalas vs aalsu, p.47); derivational (krt/taddhita) suffixed forms follow the same rules (kari, karto, baapdo, karnaar); compound words stress each member separately (gujraati, baarvatiyo); pitch (rise-fall) accent is wholly sentence-level and meaning-governed; p.49: a pitch rise entails stress but stressed syllables need not carry a rise. Vyas 1967 p.133 (North Bhili, Dungarpur) independently: 'Stress is not distinctive.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('shabdagat svaraghaat') stress on citation forms, explicitly distinguished from sentence-level pitch accent; author is a native of the Vagad region describing Vagdi of Dungarpur-Banswara.
new_statements.identity_note: Joshi 1964 describes 'Vāgaṛī' (Vagdi/Wagdi) of the Vagad region (Dungarpur and Banswara districts, S Rajasthan) = Glottolog wagd1238 [wbr]; the author treats it as a boli related to Gujarati/Bhili and writes examples in Devanagari. Vyas 1967's 'North Bhili' is the Bhili of villages around Dungarpur (Vank, Nalwa, Mandav), i.e. the same Wagdi area, though he does not use the name Wagdi. Mukherjee 2011 (LSI-Rajasthan) explicitly equates his informants' Bhili of Dungarpur/Banswara with Wagdi.

readall_conflicts: No real disagreement. Joshi 1964 (ch.2 pp. 46-49, the catalog's source) gives explicit placement rules for a stress he himself calls weak and mobile; Vyas 1967 says 'Stress is not distinctive' for both his Central Bhili (Sukhsar/Jhalod, p. 28 — a different variety) and his North Bhili (Dungarpur = Wagdi area, p. 133, held earlier) and gives no placement. A non-contrastive stress whose position is predictable from syllable weight is exactly what Joshi describes, so Vyas refines rather than contradicts; the other sources (LSI-Rajasthan 2011, Phillips 2012, Grierson 1907, and all newly opened Joshi and Vyas chapters) are silent.
